title: Reveal Cards In Increasing Order
description: Brute force to optimized: an O(n^2) list simulation versus an O(n log n) true queue that simulates the reveal process on positions.

blocks.text: You have a deck of cards, each with a unique integer. Starting face down, you repeatedly: reveal the top card and remove it; if cards remain, move the new top card to the BOTTOM of the deck; repeat until all cards are revealed. Return an ordering of the deck (the arrangement to START with, top of deck first) such that revealing cards this way produces them in strictly INCREASING order.

blocks.caption: Simulating the exact reveal-and-skip process on POSITIONS (not values) directly determines which original position should hold each ascending value

blocks.text: Rather than trying to guess an arrangement and check whether it reveals in increasing order (inefficient trial and error), the exact reveal-and-skip process can be simulated directly on POSITIONS (0 through n-1): whichever position would be revealed FIRST should receive the SMALLEST value, whichever position is revealed SECOND should receive the SECOND smallest, and so on.

blocks.title: Analogy: Assigning Seat Numbers So That Calling Them in a Specific Pattern Reads Off Increasing Numbers
blocks.text: Imagine needing to assign numbered stickers to seats so that calling out seats in a specific repeating pattern (call one, skip one, call one, skip one...) reads the stickers off in increasing order. Rather than guessing which sticker goes where, simulating the EXACT calling pattern directly on the SEATS (not the stickers) reveals precisely which seat gets called first, second, third, and so on; assigning the smallest sticker to whichever seat is called first, the next-smallest to whichever is called second, and so on, solves it directly.

blocks.text: Before attempting to construct the answer by trial and error (testing candidate arrangements against the reveal process), notice that the reveal process can be simulated directly and DETERMINISTICALLY on POSITIONS, since the actual VALUES don't affect which positions get revealed when.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The desired output (increasing values) is already known: it is simply the SORTED version of the input values.

Observation 2: The reveal-then-skip PROCESS itself depends only on positions/order, not on the actual values held at each position, so it can be simulated purely on position indices (0 through n-1) independently of what values will eventually be assigned.

Observation 3: Simulating this process on a QUEUE of positions directly reveals the exact ORDER in which positions get revealed: dequeue a position (it gets revealed next), then if positions remain, dequeue-and-requeue the next one (simulating the "move to the bottom" skip).

Observation 4: Assigning the SORTED values to positions in EXACTLY this revealed order (smallest value to the first-revealed position, and so on) directly produces the correct starting arrangement.
This is a queue simulation of the reveal process, run on POSITIONS rather than values, with sorted values assigned in the exact order positions get revealed.
Simulate the exact reveal-then-skip process using a plain list of remaining positions, removing from the front (an O(n) operation on a plain list) and appending to the back as needed.

items: Sort the deck's values, since this is exactly the order values need to be revealed in.

Maintain a list of remaining positions (0 through n-1). Repeatedly alternate between "reveal" (assign the next sorted value to the front position, then remove it) and "skip" (move the front position to the back), continuing until every position has been assigned.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Explicitly alternating "reveal" and "skip" phases directly mirrors the problem's exact described process, applied to positions instead of values.
Using a plain list means removing from the front costs O(n) each time, making the overall simulation less efficient than necessary.

blocks.text: Correctly determines the arrangement, since it directly and faithfully simulates the exact process described in the problem, applied to positions.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n^2) in the worst case, due to repeated O(n) front-removal operations on a plain list.
Space: O(n), for the positions list and result array.
Limitation: using a plain list for front removal is unnecessarily slow; a true queue (deque) supports the identical simulation in O(1) per operation.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force uses a plain list, incurring O(n) cost per front removal. Instead, use an actual queue (deque) of positions, supporting O(1) removal from the front and O(1) addition to the back. The simulation logic is otherwise identical: dequeue a position (assign the next sorted value to it), then if positions remain, dequeue-and-immediately-requeue the next one (the skip step).

Sort the deck's values. Initialize a deque with positions 0 through n-1. For each sorted value (in ascending order): dequeue the front position and assign it this value in the result array; if the deque is non-empty, dequeue its new front and immediately requeue it at the back (simulating the skip).
Use an actual queue of positions to efficiently simulate the reveal-then-skip process, assigning sorted values in the exact order positions get revealed.

codes.python:
from collections import deque

def deck_revealed_increasing(deck):
    n = len(deck)
    sorted_deck = sorted(deck)
    positions = deque(range(n))                                            # positions still needing a value, in original order
    result = [0] * n
    for val in sorted_deck:                                                # assign values in ASCENDING order, since they reveal in that order
        pos = positions.popleft()                                          # this position gets the next (smallest remaining) value
        result[pos] = val
        if positions:
            positions.append(positions.popleft())                         # simulate the "move next card to the bottom" skip step
    return result


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(deck_revealed_increasing([17, 13, 11, 2, 3, 5, 7]))

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n), dominated by sorting; the queue simulation itself is O(n).
Space: O(n), for the queue and result array.

Since the reveal-then-skip PROCESS is entirely determined by position order (not by the values themselves), simulating it purely on positions reveals the EXACT sequence in which the final arrangement's positions will be uncovered. Assigning the smallest sorted value to whichever position is revealed FIRST, the next-smallest to whichever is revealed SECOND, and so on, guarantees that when the real process later runs on the actual VALUES placed at these positions, it will reveal them in exactly ascending order, by construction.

The skip step's conditional check (only if positions remain) correctly avoids an unnecessary operation on the very last remaining position.

blocks.text: When a problem describes a specific PROCESS and asks for the starting arrangement that would produce a desired OUTPUT order, simulating that exact process on POSITIONS (independent of values) directly reveals the correct assignment, without any need for trial and error.

items: Simulating the process on the actual VALUES instead of positions, which conflates "what order things are revealed in" with "what the final arrangement looks like," making the problem much harder to reason about directly.
Using a plain list/array instead of an actual queue, incurring unnecessary O(n) cost per front-removal operation.
Forgetting to check whether positions remain before performing the "skip" step, which could cause an error attempting to operate on an empty queue.

items: Explicitly stating "simulate the process on POSITIONS, not values, since the process itself doesn't depend on the values" is the key reframing that makes this problem's solution clear and direct.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Find the STARTING arrangement that produces a desired OUTPUT order via a specific process" points toward simulating that process on POSITIONS (or indices) rather than the actual values.

items: How would this change if the desired output order were DECREASING instead of increasing? Simply sort the values in descending order before assigning them to positions in the same simulated reveal order.

How would you verify your answer is correct without a separate checking function? Run the EXACT SAME reveal-then-skip process, but on the final constructed array's VALUES this time, confirming it produces the sorted sequence.
What if the "skip" step skipped TWO cards instead of one? The exact same position-simulation technique applies directly, just adjusting the simulation's skip logic to match the new rule.

A "simulate the process on positions/indices, then map sorted values onto the resulting order" technique, distinct from more typical direct-simulation queue problems elsewhere in this category, since here the process determines an ASSIGNMENT rather than a direct answer.
